book.closing: You have completed the tour of the **38 standard libs of `ridgun-libs`**!
ch.hash.desc: The **`hash`** lib implements **SipHash-1-3** (Aumasson & Bernstein) with a 128-bit key and a 64-bit result. `siphash13` hashes a whole string; the compiler's native operations `siphash13 range` and `siphash13 range low` (ridgunc 1.0.44) hash a range of bytes in some tens of nanoseconds; `siphash13 reference` is the same hash written in plain Ridgun, to read and to test against; and `siphash new key` draws a random 16-byte key from the system.
ch.hash.guarantee: A key of another length, or a range outside the data, gives `0` instead of reading out of bounds, and the native operation returns the same 64 bits as the plain-Ridgun reference for every length and offset tested.
ch.hash.honest: Let's be honest: when the hash function of a hash table is public, whoever controls the keys can send thousands that land in the same slot, and one request then costs what a million should (hash flooding).
ch.hash.subtitle: SipHash-1-3 Keyed Hashing for Hash Tables
ch.hashmap.desc: The **`hashmap`** lib implements `HashMap V`, a map from `String` keys to values of any type, built on tensors: a slot table with open addressing and linear probing, at most half full, points into dense key and value tensors kept in insertion order. Keys are hashed with SipHash-1-3 (the `hash` lib) under a random seed per map; `hashmap put`, `hashmap add`, `hashmap get` and `hashmap has` take constant expected time, and `hashmap pairs` returns the entries in insertion order.
ch.hashmap.guarantee: The map is updated in place and grows by doubling, so `n` inserts cost $O(n)$ in total; always use the map an operation returns (`ADR-0009`). A random seed per map keeps an attacker from choosing keys that collide.
ch.hashmap.honest: Let's be honest: counting words or grouping a hundred thousand records with an association list is quadratic, and an ordered tree pays a logarithm and an allocation on every insert when all you need is to find a key.
ch.hashmap.subtitle: A Hash Map from `String` Keys to Any Value, on Tensors and Seeded with SipHash
ch.mail.desc: The **`mail`** lib builds and renders **RFC 5322** messages (RFC 2047 encoded-words for non-ASCII headers, quoted-printable bodies with lines of at most 76 bytes, `multipart/alternative` when there is text and HTML) and submits them with an **SMTP** client (RFC 5321, RFC 6409) over TLS: implicit TLS on port 465 (RFC 8314) or STARTTLS (RFC 3207), with `AUTH PLAIN` or `AUTH LOGIN` (RFC 4954) sent only after the TLS handshake. Header injection is rejected when the message is rendered, and every failure is a typed `SmtpError` that says whether a retry makes sense.
ch.mail.guarantee: `mail render` rejects any header value that holds CR or LF, so user input cannot add headers, and `smtp send` never continues in cleartext: without implicit TLS the server must offer STARTTLS, and the credentials are sent only after the handshake.
ch.mail.honest: Let's be honest: sending the email that verifies an account looks like one line, until a subject with an accent arrives as question marks, a line that starts with a dot vanishes, or a form field with a line break adds a `Bcc:` header of the attacker's choice.
ch.mail.subtitle: RFC 5322 Messages and SMTP Submission over TLS
ch.tls.desc: The **`tls`** lib is a TLS client in pure Ridgun: **RFC 8446 TLS 1.3** and **RFC 5246 TLS 1.2**, with ECDHE key exchange (X25519, secp256r1) and AEAD suites only (AES-128-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), **X.509** chain validation against a bundle of root certificates, **RFC 6125** hostname verification, SNI and ALPN. It takes its primitives from `crypto` and its connections from `socket`, and it has no option that skips the chain, expiry, signature or hostname checks.
ch.tls.guarantee: Every handshake verifies the chain up to a trusted root, the validity dates, the handshake signature and the hostname, and only AEAD suites with ephemeral key exchange are offered: there is no option that turns a check off (`FR-TLS-001` AC4).
ch.tls.honest: Let's be honest: almost every service a program talks to today sits behind TLS, and linking OpenSSL to reach it brings a C dependency of half a million lines, with its own allocator and its own calendar of security fixes.
ch.tls.subtitle: TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 Client, X.509 Chain Validation, and Hostname Verification

fix.agent.desc: The **`agent`** lib builds on Ridgun's **Native Agent Model** (`agent`, `send ... to`, `receive from`, `try receive from`, `stop`) to provide request-reply combinators, blocking, non-blocking or bounded by a timeout (`agent ask`, `agent try ask`, `ask int with timeout`), batch dispatch and draining (`agent send batch`, `agent map batch`, `agent drain ready`), lifecycle inspection (`is agent alive`, `agent status`, `stop agent`), and three ready-made stateful agents: a counter, an append-only log and an in-memory key-value store.
fix.agent.subtitle: Native Actor Concurrency (`agent`, `send`, `receive`), Request-Reply Combinators, and Counter, Log and Key-Value Agents
fix.crypto.desc: The **`crypto`** lib implements in 100% pure Ridgun, on tensors: raw byte and bitwise primitives (`RGF-019`), the hashes **SHA-256**, **SHA-384**, **SHA-512**, **SHA-1** and **MD5**, **HMAC** and **HKDF**, constant-time equality (`ct equal`), **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256**, the AEAD ciphers **ChaCha20-Poly1305** (RFC 8439) and **AES-128-GCM** (NIST SP 800-38D), **X25519** key agreement, **Ed25519** and Minisign signatures, **ECDH** and **ECDSA** on P-256 and P-384, **RSA** PKCS#1 v1.5 and PSS verification, and **X.509** certificate parsing. It also offers the `argon2id` lib (`import argon2id` plus `export argon2id`), so `argon2id hash` and `argon2id verify` are available with `import crypto` alone. The ciphers, Poly1305, GHASH and the big-number arithmetic run on the whole-tensor operations of the compiler: sealing 1 MiB with `aead seal` takes about 3 ms.
fix.crypto.subtitle: Hashes, HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, AEAD Ciphers, X25519, Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA, and X.509
fix.net_agent.desc: The **`net_agent`** lib closes the loop of `ridgun-libs` by uniting **`posix`**, **`socket`**, and **`agent`**: a `ConnSlot` pairs a connection descriptor with the agent that holds its state; `conn poll step` polls the descriptor without blocking, passes what arrives to the agent and writes its reply back; `reactor sweep` does that for a whole table of connections and drops the closed ones; and `reactor shutdown` closes every descriptor and stops every agent.
fix.net_agent.guarantee: A connection that is closed or fails leaves the table on the sweep that sees it, with its descriptor closed and its agent stopped, and `reactor shutdown` does the same for all the rest, so no descriptor and no agent is leaked.
fix.net_agent.honest: Let's be honest: in a server, accepting TCP connections is the easy part; the hard part is keeping the state of each connection apart, reading and writing without blocking the others, and closing every descriptor and stopping every agent when a connection ends.
fix.net_agent.subtitle: One Agent per Connection: Non-Blocking Polling and Reactor Sweep
fix.pool.desc: The **`pool`** lib groups a fixed number of agents into an `AgentPool`: `pool ask shard` sends each request to the agent chosen by its key, so the same key always reaches the same agent; `pool broadcast` sends one message to every agent; `pool drain all` collects, without blocking, the replies that are ready; and `pool shutdown` stops all of them.
fix.pool.guarantee: The number of agents is fixed when the pool is built, so the memory of the pool is bounded, and routing by `abs(key) % size` is deterministic: the same key always reaches the same agent.
fix.pool.honest: Let's be honest: when every request for the same user or the same key must reach the same worker, and now and then one message must reach all of them, writing that routing and the orderly stop by hand in every program is repetitive and easy to get wrong.
fix.pool.subtitle: Agent Pools: Sharding by Key, Broadcast, and Non-Blocking Drain
fix.tensor.desc: The **`tensor`** lib adds, to Ridgun's native `Tensor[...]` type, the helpers that the language does not give directly: shape queries (`tensor rows`, `tensor cols`, `tensor shape`), extraction of one row or one column (`tensor row`, `tensor col`), an explicit copy (`tensor clone`), the matrix product (`tensor matmul`), and element-wise operations between two whole tensors: XOR, AND, OR, addition, subtraction and multiplication.
fix.tensor.subtitle: Shapes, Rows and Columns, Matrix Product, and Block-Wise Operations
